screens.title: Layered Architecture of a DApp
screens.narratorSegment: A DApp is best understood as a stack of responsibilities. The frontend provides the visual interface and gathers user intent. The middleware or connector layer translates that intent into blockchain calls, handling serialization, RPC interaction, and the signing workflow. The smart‑contract backend holds the authoritative rules and state and executes changes when transactions are mined. Start with a tight definition: the frontend is often built with the same web technologies you already know, but it must be able to assemble and send signed transactions. Middleware libraries such as ethers. js or web3. js provide the functions to read state and craft transactions; they integrate closely with wallets like MetaMask that hold the user's private keys. Smart contracts, typically written in Solidity for Ethereum‑compatible chains, are deployed bytecode that run deterministically on every node and therefore form the immutable business logic. A common misconception is to treat the frontend hosting location as the measure of decentralization. It is not. What matters is where the rules and state live. For example, an NFT marketplace can serve a React UI from a centralized host while ownership, transfers, and listing logic are enforced by on‑chain contracts. The practical takeaway: design the stack by answering what must be tamper‑proof versus what must be fast or cheap.

keyIdea.title: Layer rule
keyIdea.text: Place tamper‑proof rules and state on‑chain; keep fast or large data off‑chain while preserving verifiable links.

content.html:
Core Concept

Layered Architecture

A DApp separates concerns into frontend, middleware, and on‑chain backend so you can reason about trust, cost, and performance.

Frontend
  • UI, capture user actions, show contract data
  • Built with React, Vue, or Angular
Middleware / Connector
  • ethers.js or web3.js to query and sign transactions
  • Interacts with wallets and RPC nodes
Smart‑contract Backend
  • Solidity contracts enforce rules and store essential state
  • Deployed to an EVM‑compatible chain
Architecture Diagram
Frontend (React / Vue)
Handles UX and initiates reads and signed transactions.
Middleware (ethers.js / web3.js)
Encodes RPC calls, manages signing, and queries contract state.
Blockchain / Smart Contracts (Solidity)
Immutable logic and canonical state executed by the network.
Key Takeaway

Design the stack by placing only tamper‑proof rules on‑chain and keeping large or mutable data off‑chain.

screens.title: Frontend (Client‑Side) in DApps
screens.narratorSegment: The frontend looks familiar but serves additional responsibilities in a DApp. It still renders UI, gathers input, and manages state for the user experience. The difference is that it now must assemble calls that interact with decentralized contracts and trigger cryptographic signing by the user. Practically, this means integrating libraries and wallet adapters that can request signatures and broadcast transactions. Popular frontend frameworks remain the same — React, Vue, or Angular — and you can reuse existing UI patterns. But you must also be deliberate about where data lives: large assets and mutable content are usually stored off‑chain while the frontend holds references such as content hashes. A common mistake is assuming the frontend’s hosting equals centralization. Hosting can be centralized while logic and state remain decentralized. A concrete example: a React app that lists NFTs calls a smart contract to read ownership data and displays an image fetched from IPFS using a content identifier stored on the contract. Watch for UX pitfalls like waiting for transaction confirmations; plan clear feedback and avoid blocking the UI while a transaction is pending. The takeaway: treat the frontend as the user's gateway to a decentralized backend, not as the source of truth.

keyIdea.title: Frontend role
keyIdea.text: Build responsive UI and integrate with middleware and wallets so users can read state and sign transactions securely.

content.html:
Definition

Frontend (Client‑Side)

Responsible for UX, rendering blockchain data, and requesting signatures for transactions.

  • Uses familiar frameworks: React, Vue, Angular.
  • Integrates wallet adapters to prompt signature flows.
  • Fetches off‑chain assets like images from IPFS using hashes stored on‑chain.
Concrete example
A React UI reads NFT ownership from a contract and loads the artwork from IPFS using the content hash.
Sample Frontend Code (pseudo)
// Example: reading a contract and fetching IPFS image
const provider = new ethers.providers.Web3Provider(window.ethereum)
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider)
const owner = await contract.ownerOf(tokenId)
const cid = await contract.tokenURI(tokenId) // returns a content hash
// fetch image from IPFS gateway
const img = await fetch(`https://ipfs.io/ipfs/${cid}`)
Key Takeaway

Keep UX responsive and clearly communicate signing and confirmation states when the frontend triggers transactions.

screens.title: Middleware and Wallet Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the middleware and wallet flow clarifies where responsibility shifts from client code to the user and the network. The flow begins when a user requests an action — for example, buying a token. The frontend formats the required parameters and calls a library like ethers. js or web3. js. That library prepares a transaction object and asks the connected wallet to sign it. The wallet prompts the user to approve, performs the cryptographic signature using keys it controls, and returns the signed transaction to be broadcast. The library submits the signed transaction to an RPC node where miners or validators include it in a block. The middleware also supports read operations that do not require signatures; these query nodes for contract state and historical transactions. A common misconception is that middleware performs trusted computations; it does not. Middleware is an interface layer that encodes requests and reads network responses. For example, when reading a token balance the frontend can call a read function via ethers. js and immediately display the result, whereas changing ownership requires a signed transaction. The practical skill here is designing clear user feedback for pending, confirmed, and failed transactions so users never mistake a broadcast for a final state change.

keyIdea.title: Flow summary
keyIdea.text: Frontend → ethers.js/web3.js → Wallet signs → RPC node broadcasts → Blockchain finalizes state.

content.html:
Process Flow

Middleware & Wallet Flow

A stepwise transformation of user intent into a finalized blockchain transaction.

1. User action
Clicks buy, transfer, or call a function.
2. Middleware encodes
ethers.js or web3.js prepares a transaction object or read call.
3. Wallet signs & broadcasts
Wallet prompts user for signature and submits the signed tx to the network.
Supporting Notes
  • Read calls do not require signatures and are fast.
  • Signed transactions incur gas and require confirmations to finalize.
  • Middleware does not validate business logic; contracts do.
Scenario
A user approves a token swap: frontend collects parameters, ethers.js builds the tx, MetaMask signs, and the tx is relayed to an RPC node for inclusion in a block.
Common Mistake

Assuming a signed transaction is final immediately. Wait for confirmations and show clear UI state for pending, confirmed, or failed transactions.

screens.title: Smart Contracts as Backend Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts are the decentralized backend of a DApp: they encode the business rules, manage canonical state, and execute deterministically across all network nodes. When you design a contract you decide which state variables and functions must be trusted and immutable. For example, in a token contract the balance mapping and transfer logic must be on‑chain so everyone can verify ownership. Because contracts are deployed bytecode, changing them later is nontrivial; this immutability is a feature but also a constraint. Use upgrade patterns or careful design if your logic may need changes. In practice, developers write contracts in Solidity for EVM chains, compile to bytecode, and deploy to a chain such as Ethereum mainnet or a Layer 2. A common misconception is that every piece of application logic must be on‑chain. That leads to high costs and poor scalability. Instead, keep time‑sensitive or large computations off‑chain where possible, and place only those rules that require censorship resistance on‑chain. For instance, an NFT’s art file is kept off‑chain with a content hash on‑chain to prove authenticity while avoiding expensive storage costs. The takeaway is to treat smart contracts as the single source of truth for rules and state that must be verifiable by anyone.

keyIdea.title: Smart contract role
keyIdea.text: Use smart contracts for immutable, verifiable rules and canonical state; avoid putting large or mutable data directly on-chain.

content.html:
Definition

Smart Contracts

Immutable code deployed to a blockchain that enforces rules and stores canonical state.

  • Written in Solidity for EVM chains.
  • Execute deterministically on each node.
  • Manage critical state like balances, ownership, and permissions.
Analogy
Think of a smart contract as a tamper‑proof rules engine that any user can inspect and interact with under the same public rules.
Contract Example (Greeter)
// contracts/Greeter.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Greeter {
  string private greeting;
  constructor(string memory _greeting) { greeting = _greeting; }
  function greet() public view returns (string memory) { return greeting; }
  function setGreeting(string memory _newGreeting) public { greeting = _newGreeting; }
}
Key Takeaway

Place rules that require public verification and immutability on‑chain, and model state transitions as contract calls.

screens.title: Setting Up a Minimal Hardhat Project
screens.narratorSegment: A minimal local development environment lets you iterate on contracts safely. The steps in this chapter’s hands‑on activity are intentionally simple: install Node. js and npm, create a project folder, initialize npm, install Hardhat as a development dependency, and run npx hardhat to create a config. This process yields a hardhat. config. js and a node_modules folder so that you can compile contracts locally. Compiling produces artifacts including bytecode and the contract ABI. That ABI is crucial for frontend libraries to know how to encode and decode calls. If you created the Greeter. sol example and compiled it, you will find artifacts/contracts/Greeter. sol/Greeter. json with the compiled output. Watch for common pitfalls: be sure your Node. js and npm versions are compatible and install Hardhat as a dev dependency rather than globally unless you have a specific environment reason. The practical example here is to compile Greeter and then inspect the resulting ABI to confirm the function signatures match what you call from ethers. js. This hands‑on step bridges theory and practice by exposing the exact contract interface your frontend will call.

keyIdea.text: A minimal Hardhat project compiles contracts and produces ABIs that frontend libraries use to call on‑chain functions.

content.html:
Process

Hardhat Quick Setup

Follow the hands‑on steps to scaffold a local development environment for smart contracts.

1. Initialize project
mkdir my-first-dapp && cd my-first-dapp; npm init -y
2. Install Hardhat
npm install --save-dev hardhat
3. Create config
npx hardhat → select create an empty hardhat.config.js
Compile Outcome
// After npx hardhat compile
you'll find:
- artifacts/contracts/Greeter.sol/Greeter.json
- abi and bytecode inside the JSON

// Frontend uses ABI to build contract instance
const contract = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider)
Key Takeaway

Compiling produces the ABI that bridges contracts and frontend code; use a local Hardhat environment to iterate safely before deployment.

screens.title: On‑Chain vs Off‑Chain Components
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding what to place on‑chain versus off‑chain is a central design choice. On‑chain components — smart contracts, token balances, and transaction history — enjoy decentralization, immutability, and public verifiability. These features matter for assets and rules that require trustless enforcement, such as token transfers or ownership records. The downside is cost and scalability: storing and modifying data on the blockchain consumes gas and can be slow. Off‑chain components, like frontend code, large media files, or heavy analytics, are far cheaper and faster. They can be hosted centrally or on decentralized storage like IPFS. The practical compromise is to keep small, essential proof data on‑chain (for example, a content hash) and store large content off‑chain. A concrete example: store an NFT's image on IPFS and only the CID on the contract. A common misconception is to equate decentralization with placing everything on‑chain; doing so quickly becomes prohibitively expensive. Instead, architect your system so that on‑chain elements provide the authoritative proofs while off‑chain components provide performance and storage efficiency. The key is ensuring off‑chain data can be verified against on‑chain references when needed.

content.html:
Comparison

On‑Chain vs Off‑Chain

On‑Chain
Immutable, verifiable, tamper‑resistant. Good for assets and rule enforcement.
Off‑Chain
Fast, cheap, and scalable. Good for large files, UI assets, and analytics.
Concrete example
Store an NFT image on IPFS and keep only the content hash on the smart contract to prove authenticity while saving cost.
Trade‑off guide
  • On‑chain: security and transparency at the cost of gas and latency.
  • Off‑chain: performance and storage efficiency with additional trust considerations.
  • Use cryptographic hashes or oracles when off‑chain data must be trusted.
Pro Tip

Keep only the minimal verifiable reference on‑chain and fetch larger content off‑chain using that reference.

screens.title: Common Tech Stack for Ethereum DApps
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable stack accelerates development and reduces decision overhead. A common Ethereum DApp stack includes React for the frontend, styled components or another C S S system for styling, and ethers. js or wagmi for blockchain interactions and utilities. On the contract side, developers write Solidity and use Hardhat or Foundry for compilation, testing, and deployment. For networks, you might choose Ethereum mainnet or a Layer 2 like Polygon based on cost and throughput needs. Wallet integrations include MetaMask or WalletConnect to handle signatures. For decentralized storage, IPFS is commonly used to host large files with content addressing. This stack covers the major roles: UI, connector libraries, contract tooling, and storage. When picking a stack, consider the trade‑offs: a Layer 2 can dramatically lower gas costs, while different frameworks offer varying integration ergonomics. A misconception to avoid is overcomplicating the stack early; choose well-supported libraries and keep the initial architecture simple. Start with the minimal stack and add components only when needed. The practical value is that you can replicate this pattern across many DApp types such as NFT marketplaces, token portals, or simple governance tools.

Core Concept

Common Tech Stack

A practical, minimal stack used by many Ethereum DApps.

Frontend
React, Styled‑components; handles UI and transaction initiation.
Middleware
ethers.js or web3.js. Use wagmi for React hooks where available.
Smart Contracts & Tooling
Solidity for contracts; Hardhat or Foundry for testing and deployment.
Storage & Wallets
IPFS for media; MetaMask and WalletConnect for user keys.
Stack Scenario
For an NFT marketplace you might use React for listings, ethers.js to call contracts that store token metadata hashes, Hardhat to test and deploy contracts, and IPFS to serve artwork.

screens.title: Where to Host Frontend & Assets
screens.narratorSegment: Hosting decisions influence availability and perceived decentralization. Frontend code can be hosted on centralized CDNs or platforms for convenience, on decentralized storage like IPFS for stronger distribution guarantees, or on hybrid approaches. The critical point is that hosting location does not alone determine whether a DApp is decentralized. What does matter is the location and execution of the application’s authoritative logic and state. For large media files such as NFT images, IPFS and similar systems provide content addressing; the smart contract stores the content hash. This approach preserves immutability of the link while avoiding the cost of on‑chain storage. Another consideration is updates: centrally hosted frontend code can be updated quickly, while decentralized hosting may be slower to modify. When designing a DApp, document which pieces need censorship resistance and place them on systems that provide it. For example, keep contract code and essential state on‑chain; host UI either centrally for rapid updates or on IPFS if censorship resistance is a priority. The takeaway is to align hosting with the required guarantees for each component rather than aiming for absolute decentralization everywhere.

content.html:
Architecture

Hosting Frontend & Assets

Choose hosting based on needed guarantees: fast updates or censorship resistance.

Centralized Host
Simple deployment and quick updates; may be vulnerable to takedown.
Decentralized Storage (IPFS)
Content addressed and persistent; pair with on‑chain content hashes for verification.
Hybrid
Host frontend centrally for rapid iteration and store critical assets on IPFS for permanence.
Scenario
An artist might publish artwork to IPFS and store the CID in a contract while serving the UI on a centralized host to iterate on marketplace features. The content remains verifiable even if the UI changes.
Key Takeaway

Choose hosting that matches your need for permanence versus agility and keep verifiable links on‑chain when necessary.

screens.title: Practical Example: NFT Marketplace Stack
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s examine a concrete example: an NFT marketplace. The frontend is a React application that lists items, lets users connect wallets, and initiates buy or list actions. Middleware uses ethers. js or wagmi hooks to query contract state such as ownership and to create and send transactions for purchases. Wallets like MetaMask prompt the user for signatures during purchase flows. Smart contracts, written in Solidity, manage token ownership, transfers, royalties, and listing data that must be canonical. Media files for artwork live on IPFS with the contract storing CIDs as immutable references. This separation allows the marketplace to verify ownership and transfers on‑chain while benefiting from IPFS storage for images. A common design error is attempting to store mutable metadata or large files directly in contract storage; use CIDs instead. Another practical consideration is network choice: deploying to a Layer 2 like Polygon can reduce gas costs for buyers. The main lesson is that each technology in the stack plays a distinct role: UI for users, middleware for connectivity, wallets for signatures, contracts for rules, and decentralized storage for large content. Design each part with that responsibility in mind.

Comparison

NFT Marketplace Stack

Frontend
React handles listings, wallet connections, and swap UI.
Middleware
ethers.js or wagmi to read contract state and send signed transactions.
Blockchain
Solidity contracts manage ownership, transfers, and royalties.
Storage
Artwork on IPFS; contract stores the CID as a reference.
Data Flow
User initiates buy → frontend assembles params → ethers.js requests wallet signature → wallet signs and broadcasts → contract transfers ownership on inclusion.
Key Takeaway

Map responsibilities clearly: on‑chain for ownership and rules; off‑chain for large assets and fast UI iterations.

screens.title: Design Checklist for DApp Architects
screens.narratorSegment: When designing a DApp, a short checklist helps you make consistent decisions. Ask: does this data require public verifiability and immutability? If yes, consider putting it on‑chain. If not, can the data be represented by a small cryptographic proof or hash that you store on‑chain instead of the full content? Next, evaluate cost: how frequently will this state change and what gas costs will that incur? For frequent updates, off‑chain approaches or Layer 2 networks may be preferable. Consider privacy and compliance: public chains expose state to anyone, so avoid putting sensitive user data on‑chain. Also decide about hosting: will the frontend be centrally hosted for rapid iteration or distributed on IPFS for permanence? Finally, prepare for failure modes: plan for transaction reverts, front‑end forks, and contract upgrades if you need fixable logic. A common misconception is to design primarily for technical elegance rather than user cost and UX; prioritize minimizing gas and avoiding unnecessary on‑chain writes. Use this checklist during design reviews to ensure each on‑chain decision is justified by security, auditability, or trustlessness. Close by asking which single component in your design most benefits from being immutable.

keyIdea.title: Design checklist
keyIdea.text: Ask about verifiability, cost, privacy, hosting, and upgradeability before placing data or logic on‑chain.

content.html:
Checklist

Design Checklist for DApps

1. Need for immutability?
Store on‑chain only if public verification or censorship resistance is required.
2. Cost & frequency
Estimate gas and prefer off‑chain for frequent or large updates.
3. Privacy concerns
Avoid storing sensitive data openly on public chains.
4. Hosting strategy
Choose between rapid updates and censorship resistance for the frontend and assets.
5. Upgradeability & failure modes
Plan for upgrades or compensating controls if bugs or exploits occur.
Key Takeaway

Use this checklist to justify on‑chain choices and reduce surprise costs while protecting user experience and privacy.

In this lesson we’ll build a clear mental model of a DApp’s layers and the technologies that sit in each layer. You will learn to name the frontend tools, the middleware connectors, and the smart-contract backend, and why each layer matters for security, cost, and user experience. I’ll show a compact example stack you can reuse, and we’ll emphasize the practical distinction between on‑chain and off‑chain components so you can decide what belongs where. For instance, you’ll see why large media files are kept off‑chain and how a frontend still interacts with on‑chain logic through wallets and RPC libraries. By the end, you will be able to diagram a simple DApp, explain which code runs on the blockchain, and outline a minimal development environment to start building. Think about a small NFT marketplace: frontend UI for listings, ethers. js to construct transactions, and Solidity contracts to manage ownership. As you move through the lesson screens, ask yourself which parts require immutability and which parts are better served off‑chain for speed and cost.

These objectives set a clear path for your learning. First, you will diagram the layers of a DApp and explain the role each layer plays in handling interface, connectivity, and on‑chain state. Knowing how to draw that diagram helps you reason about trust boundaries and deployment choices. Second, you will identify the core technologies used in each layer — for example, React for frontend, ethers. js or web3. js for middleware, and Solidity with Hardhat for smart‑contract development. Recognizing these tools helps you pick the right stack when you start a project. Third, you will explain how smart contracts act as the backend logic and state manager, including example responsibilities like transfers, ownership, and business rules. Finally, you will differentiate on‑chain versus off‑chain components: what must be stored on the ledger, and what can live off‑chain to save cost. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify practical understanding by drawing diagrams, naming tools, or initializing a minimal Hardhat project. Consider which objective you want to practice first and why it will make building safer and more efficient.

To make progress measurable, each objective pairs with a small practice task. For layer diagramming, draw a three‑box diagram and annotate where the UI, middleware, and smart contracts live. For mapping technologies, create a one‑page cheat sheet that lists frontend frameworks, middleware libraries, and smart‑contract toolchains. For smart‑contract understanding, compile and deploy a simple contract locally using Hardhat so you can observe state changes and transactions. For on‑chain versus off‑chain choices, pick a sample asset — for example an NFT image — and justify storing the file off‑chain with only a content hash on‑chain. These practices bridge theory and hands‑on skill, and they target real decisions you will make when designing a DApp. When you work through these tasks, you’ll notice common misconceptions: for instance, hosting the frontend on a centralized server does not make the entire DApp centralized if the logic and state are on‑chain. Each milestone is designed to expose that distinction clearly and to give you a short artifact you can use during code reviews or interviews.

A DApp is best understood as a stack of responsibilities. The frontend provides the visual interface and gathers user intent. The middleware or connector layer translates that intent into blockchain calls, handling serialization, RPC interaction, and the signing workflow. The smart‑contract backend holds the authoritative rules and state and executes changes when transactions are mined. Start with a tight definition: the frontend is often built with the same web technologies you already know, but it must be able to assemble and send signed transactions. Middleware libraries such as ethers. js or web3. js provide the functions to read state and craft transactions; they integrate closely with wallets like MetaMask that hold the user's private keys. Smart contracts, typically written in Solidity for Ethereum‑compatible chains, are deployed bytecode that run deterministically on every node and therefore form the immutable business logic. A common misconception is to treat the frontend hosting location as the measure of decentralization. It is not. What matters is where the rules and state live. For example, an NFT marketplace can serve a React UI from a centralized host while ownership, transfers, and listing logic are enforced by on‑chain contracts. The practical takeaway: design the stack by answering what must be tamper‑proof versus what must be fast or cheap.

The frontend looks familiar but serves additional responsibilities in a DApp. It still renders UI, gathers input, and manages state for the user experience. The difference is that it now must assemble calls that interact with decentralized contracts and trigger cryptographic signing by the user. Practically, this means integrating libraries and wallet adapters that can request signatures and broadcast transactions. Popular frontend frameworks remain the same — React, Vue, or Angular — and you can reuse existing UI patterns. But you must also be deliberate about where data lives: large assets and mutable content are usually stored off‑chain while the frontend holds references such as content hashes. A common mistake is assuming the frontend’s hosting equals centralization. Hosting can be centralized while logic and state remain decentralized. A concrete example: a React app that lists NFTs calls a smart contract to read ownership data and displays an image fetched from IPFS using a content identifier stored on the contract. Watch for UX pitfalls like waiting for transaction confirmations; plan clear feedback and avoid blocking the UI while a transaction is pending. The takeaway: treat the frontend as the user's gateway to a decentralized backend, not as the source of truth.

Understanding the middleware and wallet flow clarifies where responsibility shifts from client code to the user and the network. The flow begins when a user requests an action — for example, buying a token. The frontend formats the required parameters and calls a library like ethers. js or web3. js. That library prepares a transaction object and asks the connected wallet to sign it. The wallet prompts the user to approve, performs the cryptographic signature using keys it controls, and returns the signed transaction to be broadcast. The library submits the signed transaction to an RPC node where miners or validators include it in a block. The middleware also supports read operations that do not require signatures; these query nodes for contract state and historical transactions. A common misconception is that middleware performs trusted computations; it does not. Middleware is an interface layer that encodes requests and reads network responses. For example, when reading a token balance the frontend can call a read function via ethers. js and immediately display the result, whereas changing ownership requires a signed transaction. The practical skill here is designing clear user feedback for pending, confirmed, and failed transactions so users never mistake a broadcast for a final state change.

Smart contracts are the decentralized backend of a DApp: they encode the business rules, manage canonical state, and execute deterministically across all network nodes. When you design a contract you decide which state variables and functions must be trusted and immutable. For example, in a token contract the balance mapping and transfer logic must be on‑chain so everyone can verify ownership. Because contracts are deployed bytecode, changing them later is nontrivial; this immutability is a feature but also a constraint. Use upgrade patterns or careful design if your logic may need changes. In practice, developers write contracts in Solidity for EVM chains, compile to bytecode, and deploy to a chain such as Ethereum mainnet or a Layer 2. Instead, keep time‑sensitive or large computations off‑chain where possible, and place only those rules that require censorship resistance on‑chain. For instance, an NFT’s art file is kept off‑chain with a content hash on‑chain to prove authenticity while avoiding expensive storage costs. A minimal local development environment lets you iterate on contracts safely. The steps in this chapter’s hands‑on activity are intentionally simple: install Node. js and npm, create a project folder, initialize npm, install Hardhat as a development dependency, and run npx hardhat to create a config. That ABI is crucial for frontend libraries to know how to encode and decode calls. If you created the Greeter. sol example and compiled it, you will find artifacts/contracts/Greeter. sol/Greeter. json with the compiled output. Watch for common pitfalls: be sure your Node. js and npm versions are compatible and install Hardhat as a dev dependency rather than globally unless you have a specific environment reason. The practical example here is to compile Greeter and then inspect the resulting ABI to confirm the function signatures match what you call from ethers. js. This hands‑on step bridges theory and practice by exposing the exact contract interface your frontend will call.

Off‑chain components, like frontend code, large media files, or heavy analytics, are far cheaper and faster. They can be hosted centrally or on decentralized storage like IPFS. Instead, architect your system so that on‑chain elements provide the authoritative proofs while off‑chain components provide performance and storage efficiency. The key is ensuring off‑chain data can be verified against on‑chain references when needed.
